prompt: How do the two enantiomers of a chiral molecule usually compare?

choices.text: They have the same physical properties but different biological properties
They have different physical properties but the same biological properties
choices.why: That is the reverse. Enantiomers share physical properties such as melting point; it is their biological effects that usually differ.

choices.text: They have the same physical and the same biological properties, since they contain the same atoms and bonds
choices.why: Same atoms and bonds don't guarantee the same biological effect: chiral receptors can tell the two enantiomers apart.

choices.text: They have different physical and different biological properties
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same physical properties; it is their biological properties that usually differ.

explanation: Although the different enantiomers of a chiral molecule have the same physical properties, they usually have different biological properties. A change in chirality can affect the biological properties of many drugs, such as fluoxetine.

prompt: Which statement about fluoxetine (Prozac) matches the text?

choices.text: The racemic drug is an effective antidepressant with no activity against migraine, but the pure S enantiomer works remarkably well in preventing migraine
Both forms prevent migraine equally, because enantiomers have the same properties
choices.why: Enantiomers share physical properties, not biological ones. Racemic fluoxetine has no activity against migraine.

choices.text: The racemic drug prevents migraine, but the pure S enantiomer is inactive
choices.why: That is the reverse: the pure S enantiomer prevents migraine, while the racemic drug has no activity against it.

choices.text: Racemic fluoxetine is ineffective as an antidepressant; only the pure S enantiomer works
choices.why: Racemic fluoxetine is described as an effective antidepressant. The difference shows up for migraine.

explanation: Racemic fluoxetine is an effective antidepressant but has no activity against migraine. The pure S enantiomer, however, works remarkably well in preventing migraine: an example of how chirality affects a drug's biological properties.

prompt: Why do different enantiomers often have different biological effects?

choices.text: Biological receptors are chiral, so only one enantiomer fits a receptor's complementary shape
One enantiomer is always more stable and reacts faster in any environment
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same energy and physical properties. The difference appears only when they meet something chiral, such as a receptor.

choices.text: Enantiomers have different molecular formulas
choices.why: Enantiomers have the same formula and the same connections; they differ only in handedness.

choices.text: Receptors are achiral, so they can bind either enantiomer equally
choices.why: If receptors were achiral, the two enantiomers would bind equally and act the same. Receptors are chiral.

explanation: To have a biological effect, a substance typically must fit into an appropriate receptor that has a complementary shape. Because biological receptors are chiral, only one enantiomer of a chiral substrate can fit, just as only a right hand fits into a right-handed glove.

prompt: In the hand-and-glove analogy for a chiral receptor, what does a left hand in a right-handed glove represent?

choices.text: The mirror-image enantiomer, which is a misfit in the receptor
The enantiomer that fits the receptor and has the biological effect
choices.why: The fitting enantiomer is the right hand in the right-handed glove. The left hand is the mismatched mirror image.

choices.text: An achiral molecule, which fits any receptor
choices.why: A hand is chiral; the left hand stands for the other enantiomer of the chiral substrate.

choices.text: A racemic mixture
choices.why: A racemic mixture would be a pile of left and right hands together. A single left hand is one enantiomer.

explanation: Because biological receptors are chiral, only one enantiomer of a chiral substrate can fit, just as only a right hand can fit into a right-handed glove. The mirror-image enantiomer will be a misfit, like a left hand in a right-handed glove.

prompt: In the model of Figure 5.12.1, where a hand stands for a chiral receptor (thumb, palm and pinkie), how many binding sites does the receptor have?
explanation: In Figure 5.12.1 the fitting enantiomer is held at three places: the green substituent at the thumb, the red one at the palm and the gray one at the pinkie, with the blue substituent exposed. Section 5.12 describes the chiral enzyme receptor as having three binding sites.

prompt: In Figure 5.12.1, why can't the second enantiomer fit the hand?

choices.text: When its green and gray substituents meet the thumb and pinkie, the palm ends up holding the blue substituent instead of the red one
It has different substituents from the first enantiomer
choices.why: Enantiomers carry the same four substituents (green, red, gray and blue); only their arrangement in space is mirrored.

choices.text: It is larger than the first enantiomer
choices.why: Enantiomers are the same size. The problem is the mirrored arrangement, not size.

choices.text: It can't reach the thumb at all
choices.why: The green thumb and gray pinkie can interact appropriately; the mismatch shows up at the third site, the palm.

explanation: In Figure 5.12.1a one enantiomer fits perfectly: green at the thumb, red at the palm, gray at the pinkie, with blue exposed. In Figure 5.12.1b, when the green thumb and gray pinkie interact appropriately with the other enantiomer, the palm holds the blue substituent rather than the red one, leaving red exposed.

prompt: Ethanol is achiral, yet yeast alcohol dehydrogenase removes only one of the two hydrogens on its −CH2OH carbon. How is this possible?

choices.text: The chiral enzyme holds ethanol so that one hydrogen sits in a binding site while the other is exposed for reaction
The two hydrogens are chemically different even in ordinary solution
choices.why: Without a chiral environment the two hydrogens are chemically identical. They become distinct only when held by the chiral enzyme.

choices.text: The enzyme first converts ethanol into a single enantiomer
choices.why: Ethanol has no enantiomers; the enzyme distinguishes the two hydrogens of the achiral molecule directly.

choices.text: The enzyme removes both hydrogens at random, and the products are separated afterward
choices.why: The reaction occurs with exclusive removal of the pro-R hydrogen; there is no random removal to sort out.

explanation: Imagine the chiral enzyme receptor has three binding sites. When the green and gray substituents of the prochiral substrate are held appropriately, only one of the two red substituents (the pro-S one) is also held, while the other, pro-R, is exposed for reaction.

prompt: In the three-site model for yeast alcohol dehydrogenase acting on ethanol, which of ethanol's two −CH2OH hydrogens is held in a binding site, and which is exposed?

choices.text: The pro-S hydrogen is held; the pro-R hydrogen is exposed for reaction
The pro-R hydrogen is held; the pro-S hydrogen is exposed for reaction
choices.why: The enzyme removes the pro-R hydrogen, so that is the one left exposed. The pro-S hydrogen occupies the binding site.

choices.text: Both hydrogens are held, and neither reacts
choices.why: Only one of the two hydrogens is held. The other must be exposed, since the enzyme does remove a hydrogen.

choices.text: Both hydrogens are exposed and react equally
choices.why: Equal reaction would happen without a chiral environment. The enzyme removes only the pro-R hydrogen.

explanation: When the green and gray substituents of the prochiral substrate are held appropriately, only one of the two red substituents (the pro-S one) is also held, while the other, pro-R, substituent is exposed for reaction. This fits the observed exclusive removal of the pro-R hydrogen from ethanol.

prompt: In the reaction of ethanol with NAD⁺ catalyzed by yeast alcohol dehydrogenase, where does the transferred hydrogen add to NAD⁺?

choices.text: Only to the Re face of the NAD⁺ carbon
Only to the Si face of the NAD⁺ carbon
choices.why: The addition occurs only on the Re face.

choices.text: To both faces equally
choices.why: The enzyme provides a chiral environment, so the two faces are not equally accessible; addition is to the Re face only.

choices.text: To the oxygen of ethanol
choices.why: The hydrogen is removed from ethanol's carbon and adds to the NAD⁺ carbon.

explanation: The reaction occurs with exclusive removal of the pro-R hydrogen from ethanol and with addition only to the Re face of the NAD⁺ carbon, as described at the end of Section 5.11.

prompt: What does it mean to say an enzyme's receptor provides a chiral environment for a prochiral substrate?

choices.text: Held in the receptor, two seemingly identical groups on the substrate become chemically distinctive
The receptor converts the substrate into a chiral molecule before it binds
choices.why: The substrate stays achiral while it is held. The chiral surroundings make its two identical groups distinguishable.

choices.text: The receptor binds both enantiomers of the substrate equally
choices.why: A prochiral substrate is achiral and has no enantiomers; and a chiral receptor tends to tell mirror images apart rather than treat them equally.

choices.text: The receptor is achiral but the solvent around it is chiral
choices.why: It is the receptor itself that is chiral and creates the chiral environment.

explanation: In the absence of a chiral environment, the two red substituents of a prochiral substrate are chemically identical, but in the presence of a chiral environment, they are chemically distinctive (Figure 5.12.2a).

prompt: Without any chiral environment, how do the pro-R and pro-S hydrogens on ethanol's −CH2OH carbon compare chemically?

choices.text: They are chemically identical
The pro-R hydrogen always reacts faster
choices.why: The pro-R hydrogen is preferred only inside the chiral enzyme. Without a chiral environment the two are chemically identical.

choices.text: The pro-S hydrogen always reacts faster
choices.why: Without a chiral environment neither hydrogen is favored; the labels only name their positions.

choices.text: They differ because one is ¹H and the other is ²H
choices.why: Both are ordinary ¹H. Deuterium replacement is only imagined, to assign the pro-R and pro-S labels.

explanation: In the absence of a chiral environment, the two seemingly identical substituents on a prochiral center are chemically identical; only in the presence of a chiral environment, such as an enzyme, are they chemically distinctive (Figure 5.12.2a).

prompt: Why is a coffee mug, by itself, achiral?

choices.text: It has a plane of symmetry
It has a handle
choices.why: The handle doesn't make it chiral: a plane through the handle cuts the mug into mirror-image halves.

choices.text: It is hollow
choices.why: Being hollow has nothing to do with chirality; what matters is the plane of symmetry.

choices.text: It isn't; a coffee mug is chiral
choices.why: The text describes the mug as achiral because it has a plane of symmetry. It is your hand that is chiral.

explanation: By itself, the mug has a plane of symmetry and is achiral. When you pick it up, your hand provides a chiral environment (Figure 5.12.2b).

prompt: When you pick up an achiral coffee mug by its handle, why is one side easier to drink from than the other?

choices.text: Your hand provides a chiral environment, so the two sides of the mug become distinguishable
Picking it up makes the mug itself chiral
choices.why: The mug keeps its plane of symmetry; what changes is its surroundings, your chiral hand.

choices.text: The two sides of the mug were different all along
choices.why: By itself the mug is symmetrical; the sides are equivalent until a chiral hand holds it.

choices.text: The mug becomes a racemic mixture
choices.why: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of enantiomers; a single achiral object can't become one.

explanation: When you pick up the mug, your hand provides a chiral environment so that one side becomes much more accessible and easier to drink from than the other (Figure 5.12.2b). In the same way, a prochiral molecule held in a chiral environment has two distinguishable substituents (Figure 5.12.2a).
